    CPINSIncident app for bomb squads

    Designing for a package that might be a bomb

    Bomb squads needed one place to report a suspect package, alert the squads around it and see it through to resolution. I led the design of CPINS, the app technicians use on scene, and of the admin portal we proposed to keep the network closed to outsiders.

    Role
    Lead product designer
    Company
    People10 Technosoft
    Team
    My manager and me, with the developers
    Platforms
    Mobile app and admin web portal
    Year
    2018 to 2019
    Status
    Handed off to development
    View as

    The problem

    The client needed squads to log suspect packages in a structured way, pull in nearby squads and record how each one ended. The information is sensitive, so the system had to stay closed to the public.

    What I did

    With my manager, proposed the design process and got it agreed. Researched the context, defined roles and permissions, worked through every flow on the whiteboard with the team and developers, then designed both products: structure, flows, screens and guidelines.

    What I handed off

    A mobile app with eight core features for technicians and non-technicians, an admin web portal for accounts and squads, and visual guidelines for both.

    Key decisions Tap, don't type One action at a time Three status colours Follow only what's yours Closed by design

    A suspect package could be a bomb.

    Until it is cleared, every detail about it matters: where it is, what it looks like, who has seen it and what has been done. CPINS moves those details to the squads that need them, quickly, and to nobody else.

    Fast to report, closed to outsiders, clear about status

    One package, start to finish

    An incident moves through five moments and three statuses. The status is the one thing every squad has to read correctly, so it travels with the incident everywhere it appears.

    Active
    1. Step 1

      Reported

      A technician on scene logs the package. Location comes from the map, the details are taps, and up to three photos go with it.

      Technician on scene
    2. Step 2

      Alerted

      Squads subscribed to that squad or area get a notification on their phones.

      Subscribed squads
    3. Step 3

      Discussed

      Other technicians open it, read the details and comment. If the photos aren't clear, they ask for more.

      Nearby technicians
    4. Step 4

      Held

      If it can't be closed yet, it is marked pending, so nobody assumes it is over.

      Any technician
    5. Step 5

      Resolved

      Whoever acts records the outcome: a real device and what was done, or no device, a hoax or a false alarm.

      Acting technician

    What research added to the brief

    We researched how bomb squads operate and what is sensitive about their work. Five findings became rules for the design.

    What we learnedSo the designSee it in
    01

    Squads carry information that can't reach the public.

    Nobody joins the network on their own. People register, and an admin approves or rejects every request.

    Admin portalRoles
    02

    Privacy can't be left unattended.

    What you can do follows your role. Non-technicians can follow incidents but can't add or remove them.

    Roles and permissions
    03

    Correct, timely information decides outcomes.

    Reports use predefined options and carry a timestamp and a status. Every change notifies the squads that follow the incident.

    Create incidentNotifications
    04

    It is a high-risk moment, so every step must be obvious.

    One decision per screen, large tap targets, and follow-up options that appear only after you choose.

    Take action
    05

    Authorities should manage data and accounts.

    A separate admin portal takes account work out of the database and out of the field app.

    Admin portal

    05Design

    Built to be read at a glance

    The visual language is small on purpose: one action colour, three status colours, two typefaces and a set of icons that fill in when they are active.

    Colour

    From the 2018 guidelines

    12.2:1Emphasis button#0207B8. Primary actions and the chosen option.
    17.9:1Background#171717. Dark bars in the app and the admin portal.
    2.96:1Other button#969696. Secondary buttons and supporting text.
    Text colour#FFFFFF. Text on buttons and dark bars.
    Active#FF2D55
    Pending#FF9500
    Resolved#4DDDC7

    Contrast is measured against white. Status colours always sit next to a text label, never alone.

    Type

    Two families

    Take ActionArchivo Black for screen titles and every action label. Heavy and wide, so it reads at arm's length.
    Suspect package observedOpen Sans for everything you read: details, comments, notifications.
    ProceedResend notificationActions are set in capitals with open tracking, so a button never reads like a sentence.

    05The app

    One decision at a time

    Scroll through the core features. The phone is a live rebuild of the 2018 screens, re-moulded for iPhone 16 Plus, so you can tap through it at any point.

    01All incidents

    The feed

    Every incident in the squads and areas you follow, newest first. Each card leads with photos and a status, so a technician can size up an incident before opening it.

    Photos first, words second

    In the field, a picture of the package answers more than a paragraph about it.

    Brief: capture detailsBrief: let others help
    Open a card, or switch tabs at the bottom.
    02Create incident

    Tap, don't type

    Location comes from the map and the time from the clock. Everything else is a tap: package type, function, how it was identified, how it is employed and its status, plus up to three photos.

    Predefined options over free text

    Tiles are faster than typing, and they make every report read the same way. Rare fields wait under Add more details.

    Brief: capture details
    Pick tiles, add a photo, then press Create with no package type.
    03Incident detail

    Everything a second squad needs

    Status, type, time, squad, the reporting technician and a number to call with one tap. Comments and photos sit below the details.

    The next step never moves

    Take action is pinned to the bottom of every incident, in the same place each time.

    Brief: capture detailsBrief: let others help
    Post a comment, or tap the contact number.
    04Take action

    One action at a time

    Three actions: resolve the incident, ask for more information or resend the alert. Pick one, and only the options that follow from it appear.

    Short paths are hard to get wrong

    Under pressure, a long form invites mistakes. Showing one decision at a time keeps every path to three taps or fewer before Proceed.

    Nine scenarios, one screen. Pick one and watch the path.

    Ends resolvedEnds pendingStays active
    05Comments

    The conversation stays with the incident

    Every comment on an incident lives in one thread, so whoever opens it later gets the whole story without asking around.

    One thread per incident

    Context that lives in side channels gets lost between squads and shifts.

    Brief: let others help
    06Map view

    Lead with the nearest

    Nearby incidents appear as pins coloured by status. The nearest one's card is already open when the map loads.

    Answer the first question first

    On the map, the first question is what is closest. The card answers it before anyone taps.

    Brief: find packages nearby
    Tap a pin. Tap it again to open the incident.
    07Filters

    Filter by expertise

    Filter by device type, status, region, area or squad. A specialist can narrow the feed to the incidents that match what they know best.

    Let experts find their incidents

    Filtering by device type means the right technician can offer help, not just the nearest one.

    Brief: see your locations
    Tick a status, then Apply.
    08Subscriptions

    Follow only what's yours

    Technicians choose which squads, areas and regions they hear from. New users pick these straight after registering, so their first feed is already relevant.

    Less noise, lower load

    A few alerts that matter beat many that don't. Fewer interruptions leave room for the ones that count.

    Brief: see your locations
    Subscribe to a squad, then check the Subscribed tab.
    09Notifications

    What changed since you last looked

    Updates on incidents you follow or reported, grouped as New, Today, Yesterday and Older. Actions you take in this prototype show up here too.

    Group by recency

    Returning to the app, the only question is what is new. The grouping answers it in one glance.

    Brief: let others help

    Live prototype. Tap anything on the screen.

    06Admin portal

    Closed by design

    At the start, a database programmer added every account by hand. That made the squads depend on someone outside them, and squad members couldn't be trusted to add or remove each other. We proposed a separate web portal for admins.

    • No database programmer in the loop

      Every account used to be added by hand by someone outside the squads.

    • Squads don't manage each other

      Members can't add or delete other members, which protects trust and privacy.

    • Simple to run

      A web interface makes squad management straightforward and needs little outside support.

    • Out of the field app

      Admin work happens in the background, so people in the field never have to deal with it.

    07Reflect

    What I'd keep, and what I'd change

    Outcome

    The app went into development with its guidelines, and the admin portal we proposed was designed through to final screens. The brief asked for something simple enough to use in a crisis, and that one requirement settled most of our arguments.

    What held up

    1. Structure over free text

      Predefined options made reports quick to file and consistent to read, whichever squad filed them.

    2. Moving admin work out of the field app

      It kept the app about incidents and solved the trust problem at the same time.

    What I'd change now

    1. 1
      Test it in a drill

      Our reviews happened at desks. Today I would watch technicians run the core flows in a timed exercise, in their gear.

    2. 2
      Plan for no signal

      Basements and cordoned buildings drop connections. Reports should save on the device and send when the signal returns.

    3. 3
      Fix the contrast

      The grey supporting text in the cards is under 3:1 against its background, and the resolved teal #4DDDC7 is 1.68:1 on white. Status always carries a text label, but I would darken both.

    4. 4
      Agree on a measure

      Time from first sighting to the first alert is the number this product exists to shrink. I would baseline it with the client before design starts.
